question: I've been on escitalopram for about two and a half years. I'm thinking about tapering. Has the medication actually been moving the needle, or did I just get better on my own — and what would my likely trajectory look like over the next two months if I taper off now versus stay on it?

cause.name: genetic_family_liability
cause.description: Inherited and familial liability to mood, anxiety, substance-use, bipolar-spectrum, treatment-response, and stress-sensitivity traits.

indicators.name: family_psychiatric_liability_mentions
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, and `journal_text` for explicit family history of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, substance-use disorder, suicide, treatment response, or stress sensitivity. Count distinct family psychiatric liability categories mentioned. Return 0 if family psychiatric history is discussed and negative; return null if family history is not discussed.

effect.name: baseline_depression_anxiety_severity_chronicity
effect.description: Pre-treatment severity, duration, impairment, chronicity, age at onset, and diagnostic burden of the condition that led to escitalopram.

indicators.name: baseline_clinical_severity_history
indicators.how_to_measure: Across available clinical-history evidence, inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `chief_complaint`, `phq9_score`, and `gad7_score` for pre-treatment or historical depression/anxiety severity, chronicity, impairment, duration, age at onset, and diagnostic burden. Rate as low, moderate, high, or severe_chronic. Return null if no historical baseline severity evidence is available.

edges.description: Familial and genetic liability increases pre-treatment mood and anxiety disorder risk and severity.

sources.title: Sullivan, Neale, and Kendler (2000). Genetic epidemiology of major depression: review and meta-analysis.
sources.snippet: Twin and family evidence supports inherited liability for major depression.

cause.name: early_life_adversity
cause.description: Developmental adversity, maltreatment, chronic childhood stress, attachment disruption, and early socioeconomic disadvantage.

indicators.name: early_life_adversity_history
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, and `journal_text` for explicit developmental adversity, maltreatment, chronic childhood stress, attachment disruption, early socioeconomic hardship, or childhood trauma. Rate as none_documented, mild_or_uncertain, moderate, or severe. Return null if early-life history is not discussed.

edges.description: Early adversity can increase severity, chronicity, and treatment difficulty of later internalizing disorders.

sources.title: Nanni, Uher, and Danese (2012). Childhood maltreatment predicts unfavorable course of illness and treatment outcome in depression: a meta-analysis.
sources.snippet: Childhood maltreatment was associated with more persistent and less treatment-responsive depression.

cause.name: temperament_neuroticism_behavioral_inhibition
cause.description: Stable trait negative affectivity, neuroticism, harm avoidance, behavioral inhibition, and emotion-regulation style.

indicators.name: trait_negative_affectivity_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `journal_text`, and `imessage_text` for stable self-descriptions or clinician descriptions of trait worry, neuroticism, harm avoidance, behavioral inhibition, emotional reactivity, or chronic negative affectivity, distinct from a transient daily mood state. Rate as low, moderate, high, or very_high. Return null if stable temperament evidence is absent.

edges.description: Stable negative affectivity and inhibition increase liability to severe or persistent internalizing symptoms.

sources.title: Kotov, Gamez, Schmidt, and Watson (2010). Linking big personality traits to anxiety, depressive, and substance use disorders: a meta-analysis.
sources.snippet: Neuroticism showed strong associations with depressive and anxiety disorders.

effect.name: comorbid_psychiatric_vulnerability
effect.description: Stable vulnerability from comorbid anxiety, panic, OCD, PTSD, eating disorder, ADHD, substance-use liability, personality pathology, or bipolar-spectrum risk.

indicators.name: comorbid_psychiatric_diagnosis_count
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `chief_complaint`, `plan_text`, medication fields, and `journal_text` for explicit comorbid psychiatric diagnoses or stable vulnerabilities including panic, OCD, PTSD, ADHD, bipolar-spectrum risk, eating disorder, substance-use disorder, personality disorder, or trauma-related disorder. Count distinct comorbid vulnerability categories documented. Return 0 if psychiatric history is documented and no comorbidity is indicated; return null if no usable psychiatric-history evidence exists.

edges.description: Familial liability contributes to comorbid anxiety, bipolar-spectrum, and substance-use vulnerabilities.
Developmental adversity increases risk for multiple psychiatric vulnerabilities, not just the index episode.
Trait neuroticism and inhibition are common vulnerability factors for anxiety, depression, and substance-use comorbidity.

sources.title: Kotov, Gamez, Schmidt, and Watson (2010). Linking big personality traits to anxiety, depressive, and substance use disorders: a meta-analysis.
sources.snippet: Personality traits, especially neuroticism, cut across several psychiatric diagnoses.

cause.name: baseline_physical_health_burden
cause.description: Stable chronic illness, pain conditions, endocrine disease, inflammatory conditions, disability, and baseline somatic vulnerability.

indicators.name: baseline_physical_health_burden_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `chief_complaint`, vitals (`bmi`, `bp_systolic`, `bp_diastolic`, `heart_rate_bpm`, `weight_lb`), and `journal_text` for chronic illness, pain, endocrine disease, inflammatory conditions, disability, or baseline somatic vulnerability. Rate as low, moderate, high, or severe. Return null if baseline physical health burden cannot be assessed.

edges.description: Chronic illness, pain, endocrine disease, and disability can worsen pre-treatment internalizing severity and chronicity.
Psychiatric comorbidity tends to make the presenting condition more severe, impairing, recurrent, and harder to interpret.

effect.name: prior_episode_recurrence_history
effect.description: Number, spacing, and recency of prior depressive or anxiety episodes before the current taper decision.

indicators.name: prior_episode_history_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `journal_text`, and `chief_complaint` for explicit history of prior depressive or anxiety episodes, relapses, remissions, hospitalizations, or recurrence before the taper decision. Rate as none_documented, single_episode, multiple_or_recurrent, or chronic_recurrent. Return null if no prior-episode history evidence is present.

edges.description: Earlier onset, chronicity, and severe baseline illness tend to produce more recurrent episodes before tapering is considered.

sources.title: Burcusa and Iacono (2007). Risk for recurrence in depression.
sources.snippet: Prior course characteristics are major predictors of recurrence.

effect.name: natural_recovery_propensity
effect.description: Tendency for the original episode to remit or remain well without medication because of natural history, resilience, regression to the mean, and nonpharmacologic recovery.

indicators.name: natural_recovery_evidence_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `journal_text`, `mood_valence`, `phq9_score`, and `gad7_score` for evidence that symptoms improved or remained well during periods without medication change, through nonpharmacologic coping, stable life conditions, or spontaneous remission. Rate as low, moderate, or high. Return null if the available evidence cannot distinguish natural recovery or resilience from medication response.

edges.description: More chronic or severe illness lowers the chance that improvement would have occurred and persisted without medication.

sources.title: Posternak and Miller (2001). Untreated short-term course of major depression: a meta-analysis of outcomes from wait-list control groups.
sources.snippet: Some short-term spontaneous improvement occurs, but it is variable and incomplete.

cause.name: stable_socioeconomic_resources
cause.description: Relatively stable income, housing, education, job security, neighborhood safety, time flexibility, and material resources.

indicators.name: stable_resource_strain_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `journal_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `calendar_summary`, `calendar_description`, `transaction_name`, `merchant_name`, `amount_usd`, and finance category columns for stable housing, job security, insurance, financial strain, income interruption, debt pressure, time flexibility, or material resources. Rate resource strain as high_resources_low_strain, moderate_resources, strained, or severe_instability. Return null if stable socioeconomic/resource evidence is not available.

edges.description: Material stability, time flexibility, and secure living conditions make nonpharmacologic recovery more plausible.

effect.name: relapse_vulnerability
effect.description: Stable propensity for depressive or anxiety recurrence if pharmacologic protection or current stabilizing conditions are removed.

indicators.name: relapse_risk_documented_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `plan_text`, `phq9_score`, `gad7_score`, and `journal_text` for explicit clinician or patient evidence of relapse risk, residual symptoms, recurrent course, unstable remission, or concern about symptom return if medication is reduced. Rate as low, moderate, high, or very_high. Return null if no relapse-risk evidence is available.

edges.description: A recurrent history implies higher stable risk of relapse when maintenance treatment is reduced or stopped.

sources.title: Burcusa and Iacono (2007). Risk for recurrence in depression.
sources.snippet: The number of previous depressive episodes is a strong recurrence predictor.

edges.description: Chronic, severe, or impairing pre-treatment illness increases vulnerability to future relapse.
Comorbid anxiety, trauma, substance-use, and bipolar-spectrum vulnerabilities increase recurrence risk and complicate taper outcomes.
A stronger self-limited or resilient course lowers latent relapse pressure after medication reduction.

sources.title: Posternak and Miller (2001). Untreated short-term course of major depression.
sources.snippet: Untreated improvement motivates separating natural recovery from treatment effect.

cause.name: age_life_stage
cause.description: Age and life-stage context affecting depression recurrence, pharmacokinetics, medical burden, and stress ecology over the modeled period.

indicators.name: age_life_stage_evidence
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, and `journal_text` for explicit age, birth year, or life-stage context such as adolescent, college, early adult, midlife, perimenopause, older adult, retirement, or caregiving stage. Rate life-stage pharmacokinetic/recurrence context as young_adult_or_lower_age_risk, adult, midlife, or older_or_medically_vulnerable_stage. Return null if age/life stage is not explicit.

edges.description: Age and life stage shape chronic disease, pain, and somatic vulnerability before the taper decision.

cause.name: sex_reproductive_context
cause.description: Sex-linked biology and stable reproductive context shaping pharmacokinetics, hormonal variability, and relapse risk.

indicators.name: sex_reproductive_context_evidence
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `journal_text`, and medication fields for explicit sex-linked or reproductive context relevant to mood, anxiety, pharmacokinetics, or hormones, including male/female sex, menstruation, pregnancy, postpartum, contraception, menopause, testosterone/estrogen/progesterone treatment, or reproductive endocrine diagnoses. Classify as no_reproductive_context_documented, stable_context, cycling_or_hormonal_context, or pregnancy_postpartum_perimenopause_context. Return null if sex/reproductive context is not documented.

edges.description: Sex-linked biology and reproductive context can influence endocrine, pain, inflammatory, and chronic health burden.
Early adversity can contribute to later chronic health burden through stress physiology and social pathways.
Material resources affect chronic illness risk, treatment access, disability burden, and health maintenance.

effect.name: healthcare_access
effect.description: Stable access to prescribers, psychotherapy, insurance, medication supply, follow-up appointments, and urgent care.

indicators.name: healthcare_access_contact_evidence
indicators.how_to_measure: Use available provider, pharmacy, prescription, clinical visit, and psychotherapy-related evidence to assess stable healthcare access. Inspect `provider_name`, `department`, `visit_type`, `clinical_note_text`, `pharmacy_name`, `prescriber_name`, `days_supply`, `refills_remaining`, `calendar_summary`, and `transaction_name`. Rate as poor, limited, adequate, or strong. Return null if access cannot be assessed.

edges.description: Income, insurance, work flexibility, and transportation are major determinants of access to prescribers, therapy, and urgent care.

effect.name: stable_ssri_pharmacodynamic_responsiveness
effect.description: Person-specific biological and clinical sensitivity to SSRI therapeutic and adverse effects, beyond dose exposure alone.

indicators.name: ssri_responsiveness_evidence_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `plan_text`, `journal_text`, medication fields, `phq9_score`, and `gad7_score` for person-specific evidence of therapeutic or adverse sensitivity to escitalopram or other SSRIs beyond exposure alone, such as strong response at low dose, nonresponse despite adequate dose, activation, emotional blunting, or dose-related side effects. Rate as low_or_nonresponsive, uncertain, moderate_responsive, or highly_responsive. Return null if no usable SSRI responsiveness evidence exists.

edges.description: Stable biological differences partly determine therapeutic and adverse SSRI sensitivity.
Different diagnostic mixtures can alter whether escitalopram is likely to help or harm.

cause.name: cyp2c19_pharmacokinetic_capacity
cause.description: Stable pharmacogenomic and metabolic capacity affecting escitalopram clearance, especially CYP2C19 metabolizer status.

indicators.name: cyp2c19_genotype_metabolizer_evidence
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect 23andMe genotype rows using `genetic_rsid` and `genotype` for CYP2C19 variants relevant to escitalopram metabolism, especially rs4244285, rs4986893, rs12248560, and other CYP2C19 star-allele markers if present. Classify pharmacokinetic capacity as poor, intermediate, normal, rapid, or ultrarapid metabolizer when genotype evidence is sufficient; return null if relevant CYP2C19 genotype evidence is absent or insufficient.

effect.name: past_escitalopram_response_tolerability
effect.description: Historical symptom improvement, relapse prevention, side effects, and functional change while on escitalopram, reflecting drug effect plus natural recovery and expectancy.

indicators.name: past_escitalopram_response_tolerability_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `plan_text`, `journal_text`, medication fields, `phq9_score`, and `gad7_score` for historical improvement, relapse prevention, side effects, dose changes due to response/tolerability, or patient-reported benefit/harm while taking escitalopram. Rate net historical response/tolerability as poor_or_harmful, mixed_or_unclear, beneficial_with_side_effects, or clearly_beneficial_tolerated. Return null if no usable escitalopram response/tolerability history is available.

edges.description: Escitalopram metabolism affects historical exposure, side effects, and apparent effectiveness at a given dose.

sources.title: Hicks et al. (2015). CPIC guideline for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genotypes and dosing of SSRIs.
sources.snippet: CYP2C19 genotype is relevant to escitalopram dosing because it changes exposure.

edges.description: Person-specific SSRI sensitivity contributes to historical improvement and side effect patterns.

sources.title: Cipriani et al. (2018). Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder.
sources.snippet: Antidepressant efficacy is real on average but varies by drug and person.

edges.description: Natural improvement can be misattributed to escitalopram if medication began during spontaneous improvement.

sources.title: Posternak and Miller (2001). Untreated short-term course of major depression.
sources.snippet: Wait-list studies show measurable spontaneous improvement over weeks.

edges.description: Initial severity affects apparent antidepressant benefit, room for improvement, and tolerability decisions.

sources.title: Fournier et al. (2010). Antidepressant drug effects and depression severity: a patient-level meta-analysis.
sources.snippet: Medication-placebo differences varied with baseline depression severity.

effect.name: pre_taper_remission_stability
effect.description: How long and consistently symptoms were low before the taper decision, including whether remission occurred under stable or changing life conditions.

indicators.name: pre_taper_remission_stability_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect the most recent pre-taper evidence in `phq9_score`, `gad7_score`, `mood_valence`, `journal_text`, `clinical_note_text`, and `assessment_text` for duration and consistency of low symptoms before tapering is considered. Rate as unstable_or_not_remitted, partial_or_recent_remission, stable_remission, or long_stable_remission. Return null if pre-taper symptom stability cannot be assessed from available evidence.

edges.description: Historical response and tolerability help determine how stable remission is before tapering.

sources.title: Geddes et al. (2003). Relapse prevention with antidepressant drug treatment in depressive disorders: a systematic review.
sources.snippet: Continuation antidepressant treatment reduced relapse risk among responders.

edges.description: A naturally remitting course can produce stable wellness even if medication was not the active ingredient.

effect.name: pre_taper_residual_symptom_burden
effect.description: Residual depressive, anxiety, sleep, irritability, or somatic symptoms present just before tapering is considered.

indicators.name: pre_taper_residual_symptom_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect the most recent pre-taper evidence in `phq9_score`, `gad7_score`, `mood_valence`, `journal_text`, `imessage_text`, `clinical_note_text`, and `assessment_text` for residual depression, anxiety, sleep, irritability, or somatic symptoms. Rate as none, mild, moderate, or severe. Return null if pre-taper residual symptoms cannot be assessed.

edges.description: More severe or chronic baseline illness makes residual symptoms more likely after apparent response.

sources.title: Judd et al. (1998). Major depressive disorder: residual subthreshold depressive symptoms as predictor of rapid relapse.
sources.snippet: Residual subthreshold symptoms predicted faster relapse.

edges.description: Better historical response tends to leave fewer residual symptoms; poor tolerability can leave fatigue, sleep, or affective symptoms.
Residual symptoms indicate incomplete remission and can maintain vulnerability to future symptom return.

sources.title: Judd et al. (1998). Major depressive disorder: residual subthreshold depressive symptoms as predictor of rapid relapse.
sources.snippet: Residual symptoms predicted more rapid relapse.

edges.description: Longer and more stable remission lowers expected relapse risk compared with unstable or partial remission.

effect.name: duration_current_escitalopram_use
effect.description: Length of continuous escitalopram use before taper decision, including time at stable maintenance dose.

indicators.name: current_escitalopram_use_duration_proxy
indicators.how_to_measure: Use escitalopram-related `drug_name`, `medication_name`, `timestamp`, `local_date`, `days_supply`, `clinical_note_text`, and `plan_text` to estimate the length of continuous current escitalopram use before the taper decision. Prefer explicit duration statements in notes; otherwise use the span from first documented escitalopram record to the latest pre-taper escitalopram record when continuity is plausible from fills/notes. Return duration in days; return null if current-use duration cannot be estimated.

edges.description: Recurrent history makes longer maintenance use more likely.

sources.title: Geddes et al. (2003). Relapse prevention with antidepressant drug treatment in depressive disorders.
sources.snippet: Continuation treatment is especially relevant when absolute relapse risk is high.

edges.description: More severe or chronic original illness increases the chance of long-term maintenance use.
Perceived benefit and acceptable tolerability make extended use more likely.

effect.name: baseline_maintenance_dose_level
effect.description: Escitalopram maintenance dose immediately before any new taper or continuation regime begins.

indicators.name: baseline_maintenance_dose_mg
indicators.how_to_measure: Use the most recent documented escitalopram maintenance dose immediately before taper consideration. Inspect `medication_name`, `drug_name`, `medication_dose_mg`, `strength`, `clinical_note_text`, and `plan_text`; return dose in mg. Return null if no pre-taper escitalopram maintenance dose is documented.

edges.description: More severe illness and partial response can lead to higher maintenance dosing before tapering.
Historical benefit and side effects influence what dose is maintained at the start of the contrast.

effect.name: stable_withdrawal_susceptibility
effect.description: Stable person-specific susceptibility to SSRI discontinuation symptoms, distinct from the historical fact of prior withdrawal episodes.

indicators.name: withdrawal_susceptibility_history_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `plan_text`, `journal_text`, and `imessage_text` for stable susceptibility to discontinuation symptoms after missed doses, dose reductions, or stopping SSRIs. Rate as low, uncertain, moderate, or high. Return null if no usable withdrawal-susceptibility evidence exists.

edges.description: Metabolic differences can alter exposure drops after missed doses or reductions, influencing withdrawal susceptibility.

sources.title: Hicks et al. (2015). CPIC guideline for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genotypes and dosing of SSRIs.
sources.snippet: CYP2C19 genotype changes escitalopram pharmacokinetics.

edges.description: A person sensitive to SSRI pharmacodynamic changes may be more susceptible to discontinuation symptoms.
Somatic vulnerability, vestibular problems, pain, and medical illness can amplify discontinuation symptom susceptibility.

effect.name: prior_discontinuation_withdrawal_history
effect.description: History of withdrawal-like symptoms, relapse, or difficulty during previous missed doses, dose reductions, or medication discontinuations.

indicators.name: prior_discontinuation_withdrawal_history_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `plan_text`, `journal_text`, and `imessage_text` for prior withdrawal-like symptoms, relapse, or difficulty during previous missed doses, tapering, or discontinuation of escitalopram or other antidepressants. Rate as none_documented, mild_or_uncertain, moderate, or severe. Return null if prior discontinuation history is not discussed.

edges.description: Stable susceptibility helps explain why previous missed doses or reductions produced withdrawal-like reactions.

sources.title: Davies and Read (2019). A systematic review into the incidence, severity and duration of antidepressant withdrawal effects.
sources.snippet: Withdrawal effects vary substantially across people.

effect.name: neuroadaptation_dependence_state
effect.description: Physiologic adaptation to sustained SSRI exposure that can make rapid reductions destabilizing even if the original disorder is inactive.

indicators.name: long_term_ssri_adaptation_proxy
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect escitalopram-related `clinical_note_text`, `plan_text`, `medication_name`, `drug_name`, `medication_dose_mg`, `days_supply`, and `strength` for evidence of ongoing long-term escitalopram use or stable maintenance dosing. Rate adaptation proxy as none, short_or_uncertain, ongoing_maintenance, or long_term_maintenance. Return null if no escitalopram-use-duration or maintenance context is available in that day.

edges.description: Longer continuous exposure allows more physiologic adaptation to SSRI blockade.

sources.title: Horowitz and Taylor (2019). Tapering of SSRI treatment to mitigate withdrawal symptoms.
sources.snippet: Withdrawal risk is framed in relation to adaptation and nonlinear dose occupancy.

edges.description: Higher sustained maintenance dosing produces more sustained transporter blockade and adaptation before tapering.

sources.title: Meyer et al. (2004). Serotonin transporter occupancy of five selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at different doses: an [11C]DASB PET study.
sources.snippet: SSRI dose relates nonlinearly to serotonin transporter occupancy.

effect.name: withdrawal_symptom_burden
effect.description: Discontinuation symptoms after dose reduction, including dizziness, insomnia, anxiety, irritability, flu-like symptoms, nausea, and disequilibrium.

indicators.name: withdrawal_symptom_severity
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `journal_text`, `imessage_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, and `chief_complaint` for symptoms temporally attributed to missed doses, tapering, dose reduction, or discontinuation of escitalopram, including dizziness, brain zaps, disequilibrium, nausea, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, irritability, anxiety, agitation, or sensory disturbances. Rate as none, mild, moderate, or severe. Return `none` only when taper/missed-dose context is present and symptoms are explicitly absent; return null when there is no usable withdrawal-context evidence.

edges.description: Underlying discontinuation susceptibility causally affects current withdrawal burden, while prior history is treated as a marker and belief-shaper.

sources.title: Davies and Read (2019). A systematic review into antidepressant withdrawal effects.
sources.snippet: Withdrawal reactions are variable in incidence, duration, and severity.

effect.name: escitalopram_dose_taken
effect.description: Actual escitalopram amount ingested at each model tick after taper instructions and adherence are realized.

indicators.name: escitalopram_documented_dose_mg
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, use medication rows where `medication_name` or `drug_name` contains escitalopram or Lexapro. Return the last non-null `medication_dose_mg` documented for escitalopram that day, in milligrams. Return null if no escitalopram dose is documented that day. This is a documented dose proxy, not proof of ingestion.

indicators.name: escitalopram_fill_quantity
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, use pharmacy fill rows where `drug_name` or `medication_name` contains escitalopram or Lexapro. Sum the `quantity` dispensed that day. Return null if no escitalopram fill row is present in the window. This measures medication availability supporting actual dose taken, not direct ingestion.
indicators.computed_rule: None if count_true(contains_any(lower(coalesce(drug_name, medication_name, "")), ["escitalopram", "lexapro"])) == 0 else sum(quantity if contains_any(lower(coalesce(drug_name, medication_name, "")), ["escitalopram", "lexapro"]) else 0)

edges.description: The pre-taper maintenance dose sets the starting level under either continuation or taper regimes.

cause.name: counterfactual_taper_regime
cause.description: Exogenous intervention regime defining the causal contrast: taper off now versus stay on the current maintenance approach.

indicators.name: observed_taper_regime_indicator
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `plan_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `medication_action`, `medication_name`, and `drug_name` for the observed escitalopram regime. Return 1 if the evidence assigns or documents tapering/reducing/stopping escitalopram, 0 if it assigns or documents continuing the current maintenance regimen, and null if there is no escitalopram regimen evidence. Higher values represent the taper-off-now regime rather than stay-on-maintenance.

effect.name: taper_speed_dose_reduction
effect.description: Rate and size of escitalopram dose reductions, including abrupt, linear, hyperbolic, paused, or reversed taper patterns.

indicators.name: escitalopram_taper_action_flag
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect structured medication fields for escitalopram. Return 1 if `medication_action`, `plan_text`, or `clinical_note_text` explicitly contains a taper, decrease, dose reduction, stop, discontinue, or wean instruction for escitalopram; return 0 if escitalopram is discussed and the action is continue/maintain/no change; return null if escitalopram regimen evidence is absent.
indicators.computed_rule: 1 if any(contains_any(lower(coalesce(medication_action, plan_text, clinical_note_text, "")), ["taper", "decrease", "reduce", "reduction", "stop", "discontinue", "wean"]) and contains_any(lower(coalesce(medication_name, drug_name, plan_text, clinical_note_text, "")), ["escitalopram", "lexapro"])) else (0 if any(contains_any(lower(coalesce(medication_name, drug_name, plan_text, clinical_note_text, "")), ["escitalopram", "lexapro"]) and contains_any(lower(coalesce(medication_action, plan_text, clinical_note_text, "")), ["continue", "maintain", "same dose", "no change"])) else None)

indicators.name: taper_speed_instruction_intensity
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `plan_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `medication_action`, `medication_name`, and `drug_name` for the escitalopram taper plan. Classify the intended reduction speed as none_or_continue, slow_or_paused_reduction, moderate_reduction, or rapid_stop_or_large_reduction. Return null if no escitalopram taper or continuation plan is documented in the support window.

edges.description: The intervention contrast directly determines whether dose is held stable or reduced now, and how quickly reductions are attempted.
The assigned regime constrains the dose trajectory under taper-off-now versus stay-on-medication counterfactuals.

cause.name: medication_formulation_constraints
cause.description: Availability of liquid escitalopram, scored tablets, compounding, small dose increments, pill-splitting feasibility, and pharmacy constraints.

indicators.name: escitalopram_formulation_flexibility
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect escitalopram-related `form`, `strength`, `quantity`, `drug_name`, `medication_name`, `days_supply`, `clinical_note_text`, and `plan_text` for liquid availability, scored tablets, compounding, small dose increments, pill-splitting feasibility, or constraints forcing large dose steps. Rate taper flexibility as constrained_large_steps, standard_tablet_only, flexible_small_steps, or liquid_or_compounded_available. Return null if formulation constraints cannot be assessed.

edges.description: Lack of liquid, small tablets, or compounding can force larger dose steps and faster practical tapering.

sources.title: Horowitz and Taylor (2019). Tapering of SSRI treatment to mitigate withdrawal symptoms.
sources.snippet: Hyperbolic tapering can require progressively smaller dose reductions than standard tablet strengths allow.

effect.name: clinician_taper_guidance
effect.description: Prescriber recommendation, taper schedule, psychoeducation, risk stratification, and advice about pausing, reinstating, or continuing.

indicators.name: clinician_taper_guidance_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `plan_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `medication_action`, `provider_name`, `visit_type`, and medication fields for prescriber guidance about escitalopram tapering or continuation. Rate as continue_or_no_taper, cautious_slow_taper, standard_taper, or rapid_taper_or_stop. Return null if no clinician guidance about escitalopram regimen is documented.

edges.description: Access to prescribers and follow-up determines whether tapering is guided, monitored, and adjustable.

effect.name: clinical_monitoring_rescue_care
effect.description: Frequency and quality of clinical follow-up, safety monitoring, medication review, dose rescue, and crisis support.

indicators.name: clinical_contact_count
indicators.how_to_measure: Count non-null `clinical_note_text` rows within each day. This measures clinical monitoring/contact volume. Return 0 when the day has rows from other sources but no clinical note; return null only if the support window has no rows at all.

indicators.name: rescue_or_monitoring_action
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `plan_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `medication_action`, `visit_type`, `department`, `calendar_summary`, and `calendar_description` for monitoring visits, follow-up plans, medication rescue, dose reinstatement, urgent care, crisis support, safety monitoring, or advice to pause/reverse taper. edges.description: Access determines the availability of follow-up, crisis planning, medication review, and rapid rescue if symptoms worsen.

effect.name: psychotherapy_skills_use
effect.description: Use of cognitive, behavioral, mindfulness, exposure, problem solving, relapse prevention, or other psychological skills.

indicators.name: psychotherapy_or_skills_use_count
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `calendar_summary`, `calendar_description`, `visit_type`, `department`, `clinical_note_text`, `plan_text`, `journal_text`, `transaction_name`, and `merchant_name` for psychotherapy sessions or use of therapy skills such as CBT, exposure, behavioral activation, mindfulness, grounding, relapse-prevention planning, problem solving, or coping practice. effect.name: other_psychotropic_or_somatic_treatments
effect.description: Concurrent medication changes, supplements, sleep aids, anxiolytics, stimulants, hormonal treatments, or somatic treatments affecting symptoms or exposure.

indicators.name: other_treatment_change_count
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `medication_name`, `drug_name`, `medication_dose_mg`, `medication_action`, `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, and `plan_text` for non-escitalopram psychotropic medications, sleep aids, anxiolytics, stimulants, supplements, hormonal treatments, or somatic treatments that are initiated, stopped, increased, decreased, or used as needed. Count distinct non-escitalopram treatment changes or active PRN uses. sources.title: Geddes et al. (2003). Relapse prevention with antidepressant drug treatment in depressive disorders.
sources.snippet: Absolute benefit from continuation depends on baseline relapse risk.

cause.name: stable_medication_attitudes

indicators.name: stable_medication_attitude_level
indicators.how_to_measure: Inspect `journal_text`, `imessage_text`, `clinical_note_text`, and `plan_text` for stable beliefs about psychiatric medication, dependence, personal control, medical trust, stigma, sensitivity to medication narratives, or preference for/against medication, distinct from a single-day taper concern. effect.name: patient_taper_preference_beliefs

effect.name: adherence_to_regimen
effect.description: Consistency with intended dose or taper plan, including missed doses, extra doses, and reinstatement behavior.

indicators.name: medication_adherence_documented
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `clinical_note_text`, `plan_text`, `journal_text`, and `imessage_text` for evidence about taking escitalopram as prescribed, missed doses, extra doses, self-directed changes, or reinstatement. Rate adherence as poor, partial, or consistent. indicators.name: missed_or_extra_escitalopram_dose_mentions

sources.snippet: Depression is associated with poorer adherence to medical regimens.

cause.name: internalizing_symptom_burden

indicators.name: phq9_screening_score
indicators.how_to_measure: Use the `phq9_score` column directly when a PHQ-9 screening scale score is recorded. The score reflects depressive symptom burden over the prior two weeks ending at the visit date. Return null for support windows with no recorded PHQ-9 score.

indicators.name: gad7_screening_score
indicators.how_to_measure: Use the `gad7_score` column directly when a GAD-7 screening scale score is recorded. The score reflects anxiety symptom burden over the prior two weeks ending at the visit date. Return null for support windows with no recorded GAD-7 score.

sources.title: DiMatteo, Lepper, and Croghan (2000). Depression is a risk factor for noncompliance with medical treatment.

cause.description: Availability of supportive relationships, isolation, interpersonal conflict, reassurance, accountability, and belonging.

indicators.name: imessage_interaction_count
indicators.how_to_measure: Count non-null `imessage_text` rows within each day, including sent and received messages. This measures volume of interpersonal contact; higher values indicate more social connection opportunity, not necessarily support quality.

indicators.name: social_conflict_or_support_quality
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `imessage_text`, `journal_text`, `calendar_summary`, `calendar_description`, `imessage_thread`, and `imessage_note_text` for social support, belonging, reassurance, isolation, interpersonal conflict, criticism, loneliness, or relationship strain. Rate net social environment as conflict_isolation, mixed_or_low_support, neutral, or supportive. Return null if no usable social evidence is present. Higher categories indicate more support and less conflict.

edges.description: Support buffers stress whereas conflict and isolation increase perceived burden.

sources.title: Cohen and Wills (1985). Stress, social support, and the buffering hypothesis.
sources.snippet: Social support can buffer the effects of stress on health and distress.

edges.description: Belonging and support reduce distress, while isolation and conflict increase depressive and anxiety symptoms.

sources.title: Cohen and Wills (1985). Stress, social support, and the buffering hypothesis.
sources.snippet: Support affects distress directly and by buffering stress.

edges.description: Symptoms can cause withdrawal, reassurance seeking, irritability, and conflict, changing later social support.

sources.title: Hammen (2005). Stress and depression.
sources.snippet: Depression can generate interpersonal stress that feeds back into symptoms.

edges.description: Stable resources shape opportunities for support, time flexibility, living conditions, and interpersonal strain.
Stable interpersonal style and negative affectivity can influence conflict, isolation, and support mobilization.
Supportive relationships increase social and rewarding activities, while conflict and isolation reduce them.
High demands and impairment can crowd out rewarding activities or reduce perceived mastery.

effect.name: physical_illness_pain_inflammation
effect.description: Acute or chronic physical illness, pain, inflammation, fatigue, endocrine changes, and somatic symptom load during follow-up.

indicators.name: clinical_temperature_f
indicators.how_to_measure: Use `temperature_f` directly from clinical visit vitals. Average values within the day. Higher temperature indicates more acute illness/inflammatory burden. Return null if not recorded.

indicators.name: sleep_average_heart_rate_bpm
indicators.how_to_measure: Use `average_heart_rate_bpm` directly from Oura sleep records. Average values within the day. Higher sleeping heart rate can indicate higher physical strain, illness, pain, or inflammation burden.

indicators.name: illness_pain_symptom_severity
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `journal_text`, `imessage_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `chief_complaint`, and `assessment_text` for acute or chronic illness, pain, inflammation, fatigue, infection symptoms, injury, endocrine symptoms, or somatic symptom burden. Rate as none, mild, moderate, or severe. Return `none` only when usable health/symptom evidence is present and indicates absence of such symptoms; return null when no usable health evidence is present.

edges.description: Chronic medical conditions and pain vulnerability set somatic burden during follow-up.
Pain, inflammation, and illness disturb sleep and circadian regularity.
Pain, inflammation, fatigue, and medical symptoms can worsen mood and anxiety and be confused with medication or withdrawal effects.

sources.title: Bair, Robinson, Katon, and Kroenke (2003). Depression and pain comorbidity: a literature review.
sources.snippet: Pain and depression commonly co-occur and worsen one another.

edges.description: Poor sleep can increase pain sensitivity, inflammation, fatigue, and somatic vulnerability.
Stress can increase coping-motivated alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, sedative, or stimulant use.
Distress can increase substance use as self-medication, changing later sleep and mood.

sources.title: Boden and Fergusson (2011). Alcohol and depression.
sources.snippet: Alcohol problems and depression have reciprocal and causal interpretations in longitudinal evidence.

edges.description: Substances and rebound states can disrupt sleep architecture, timing, and next-day arousal.
Intoxication, withdrawal, rebound anxiety, and sleep effects can worsen depressive and anxiety symptoms.

sources.title: Boden and Fergusson (2011). Alcohol and depression.
sources.snippet: Alcohol use and depressive symptoms can influence each other over time.

edges.description: Substance-use liability and externalizing or anxiety comorbidity increase likelihood of substance-related mood effects.

effect.name: hormonal_state_changes
effect.description: Short-run reproductive, menstrual, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopausal, thyroid, or other hormonal variation relevant to mood and anxiety.

indicators.name: hormonal_change_mention
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `journal_text`, `imessage_text`, `clinical_note_text`, `assessment_text`, `plan_text`, and medication fields for explicit reproductive, menstrual, PMS/PMDD, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopausal, thyroid, hormonal contraception, testosterone/estrogen/progesterone, or other hormone-related changes relevant to mood or sleep. Return 1 if an active hormonal state change is explicitly present, 0 only if hormone/cycle/endocrine status is discussed and no active change is indicated, and null if there is no usable hormonal evidence.

edges.description: Stable reproductive context determines which hormonal fluctuations are plausible during the two-month window.
Hormonal shifts can disturb sleep through thermoregulation, arousal, pain, or circadian changes.
Reproductive, thyroid, or other hormonal shifts can alter mood, anxiety, and irritability during follow-up.
Other medication or somatic treatment changes can improve or worsen mood and anxiety independently of escitalopram tapering.
Monitoring data and follow-up update clinician recommendations about continuing, slowing, pausing, or reinstating.
Clinical contact can initiate or change adjunctive treatments for sleep, anxiety, mood, or medical contributors.
Monitoring can route the person into therapy, structured relapse-prevention work, or more active coping-skills use.

effect.name: expectancy_nocebo_placebo
effect.description: Symptom change driven by expectations, attention to sensations, treatment meaning, nocebo concerns, and perceived medication protection.

indicators.name: taper_nocebo_concern_severity
indicators.how_to_measure: Within each day, inspect `journal_text`, `imessage_text`, `clinical_note_text`, and `plan_text` for expectations or interpretations about tapering or continuing escitalopram: fear of relapse, fear of withdrawal, symptom vigilance, reassurance from clinician, confidence, or belief that medication is protective. Rate nocebo/threat expectancy as none, mild, moderate, or severe. Return `none` only when taper/medication expectation evidence is present and indicates confidence or low concern; return null when no usable expectation evidence is available.

edges.description: Beliefs that tapering is dangerous, liberating, protective, or harmful can create nocebo or placebo pathways.

sources.title: Colloca and Miller (2011). Role of expectations in health.
sources.snippet: Expectations are central mechanisms in placebo and nocebo effects.

edges.description: Clinician framing can reduce catastrophic interpretation or increase confidence, changing expectancy-mediated symptoms.

sources.title: Colloca and Miller (2011). Role of expectations in health.
sources.snippet: Clinical communication and expectations influence placebo and nocebo responses.

edges.description: Stable medication beliefs and trust shape how sensations during tapering are interpreted.
Expectancy can change experienced anxiety, mood, somatic distress, and symptom vigilance.

sources.title: Colloca and Miller (2011). Role of expectations in health.
sources.snippet: Expectations can generate beneficial or adverse health experiences.

edges.description: Worsening symptoms prompt more clinical contact, safety monitoring, and treatment adjustment.
Severe depression or anxiety can increase suicidal ideation, self-harm risk, agitation, or crisis-level impairment.
Intoxication and withdrawal states can increase impulsivity, agitation, and safety risk.
Severe sleep disruption can worsen agitation, impulsivity, and crisis risk.
Safety crises, agitation, and fear of losing control can worsen next-period distress and symptom burden.
Fatigue, emotional blunting, sexual dysfunction, or activation can reduce rewarding engagement and routine.
Dizziness, insomnia, nausea, anxiety, and other withdrawal symptoms can reduce activity and reward exposure.
